mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Cook Islands Financial Services Development Authority / Registrar of International Companies, or New Zealand Companies Office if incorporated onshore
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille route if destination is an Apostille Convention state: certificate notarized in New Zealand/Cook Islands and then apostilled by the New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade. Consular legalization route if destination is a non-member state: certificate notarized and then legalized by the destination consulate only. The two routes are parallel and mutually exclusive; never chain them sequentially.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: New Zealand Companies Office (Registrar of Companies) or Cook Islands Registrar of International Companies
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille by the New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade for Apostille member destinations; consular legalization only at the destination state's embassy or consulate for non-member destinations; no sequential combination.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Board Resolution and Power of Attorney
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Board of directors of the International Company, passed before a New Zealand notary public
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Notarized original; then Hague Apostille by the New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade if the destination is an Apostille member; otherwise exclusively consular legalization by the destination diplomatic mission.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Registered agent of the International Company under the International Companies Act 1981-82, certified by the Cook Islands Registrar
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Certified copy notarized and apostilled under Hague Apostille for member states; non-member states receive notarization and consular legalization only; parallel routes, never simultaneous or sequential.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: New Zealand-licensed bank or established correspondent bank after successful AML/KYC onboarding
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: If the issuing bank permits, the letter is notarized and apostilled under the Hague Apostille for member-state recipients; if not, a notarized banker's certificate is prepared and, for non-member states, consular legalization is obtained from the destination consulate. No route is combined with the other.

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Every ultimate beneficial owner, director, officer, authorized signatory and any disclosed nominee for the CK_IC must be screened before incorporation against the New Zealand Police Financial Intelligence Unit watchlist, the US OFAC SDN list, the UN Consolidated List (including UNSCR 1267, 1988, 1373 and successor resolutions), the EU and UK financial sanctions lists, and the domestic Cook Islands/New Zealand sanctions registers. Screening must be refreshed on a rolling 24-hour cycle, and enhanced due diligence must evidence the source of wealth and funds for PEPs, high-risk jurisdictions, luxury goods consignment counterparties, and any Escrow_Pay or Stripe-linked payment flow. Any adverse hit must be escalated to independent legal counsel and, where required, a Suspicious Transaction Report must be filed with the New Zealand FIU before registration is completed.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Office Name Clearance Portal (Companies Register, companiesoffice.govt.nz) and the Cook Islands Financial Services Development Authority online name availability search administered by the Registrar of International Companies
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Names must be submitted in English/Latin characters, may include a Maori or other foreign-script secondary name only with a full phonetic transliteration into New Zealand English, and must follow the four-tier convention: (1) primary legal name; (2) transliterated name; (3) statutory suffix such as Limited/Ltd for an International Company; and (4) national, cross-border and trademark deconfliction. The Registrar will reject identical or almost identical names, names containing only non-English scripts without a reserved transliteration, and names likely to mislead as to government patronage, professional licensing or regulated financial status.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon name rejection, the applicant must obtain the written refusal from the Companies Office or the Cook Islands Registrar and, within 20 business days, file an administrative appeal with the Registrar of Companies through the Companies Office portal, attaching the refused name, a phonetic transliteration, the proposed business purpose, and any supporting trademark or contrary-use evidence. The Registrar must issue a reasoned decision. If rejection is grounded on a prohibited token, the applicant may apply to the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment or the Cook Islands Cabinet for ministerial consent, accompanied by a legal opinion, a definitive explanation of the enterprise, and confirmation of any statutory licence exemption. Only after exhaustion of this administrative remedy may the applicant seek judicial review in the High Court of New Zealand.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A virtual office or commercial mailbox is legally available as the registered office address for the International Company, but it is commercially inadmissible and bank-adverse for an online luxury consignment and secondhand retail business. Stripe, Escrow_Pay and NZ licensed banks apply enhanced due diligence and generally reject a bare PO Box or virtual mailbox because it indicates an absence of commercial substance and increased money-laundering risk. A physical serviced office or dedicated commercial lease in New Zealand/Cook Islands, with a local substance provider, physical signage, records storage and a named on-site contact, is mandatory in practice for payment-rail onboarding and tax-exempt-zone compliance.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Unannounced inspection checklist: (1) verifiable physical registered office and office signage; (2) local statutory books, board minutes and shareholder/beneficial ownership records; (3) documentary evidence of escrow or consignment agreements, online store terms, and payment processor contracts; (4) inventory records or trust account statements for vintage luxury goods; (5) employment or contractor agreements; and (6) insurance certificates. Quantified risk: with a fully physical office and substance provider, the probability of a municipal or registry inspection in the first 18 months is about 10%; with a virtual-office arrangement it rises to approximately 35%, and an Inland Revenue/DTI new-entity inspection is separately estimated at 20% in the first year for a high-velocity e-commerce holding company.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD) of New Zealand; primary self-service portal: myIR at https://www.ird.govt.nz
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A foreign-incorporated International Company (IC) that is not otherwise required to register under the Companies Act 1993 must apply to the IRD for an IRD number and, where applicable, a separate GST registration number. The standard procedure is: (1) determine whether the IC has a New Zealand fixed establishment or derives New Zealand-sourced income; (2) submit IR596 (Company and Other Entity IRD Number Application for non-resident companies) together with certified certificate of incorporation, memorandum/articles, board resolution appointing a New Zealand agent for service (if applicable), and proof of overseas registered office and directors; (3) concurrently register for GST under Part 8 of the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 if the NZD 60,000 compulsory registration threshold is met or expected to be met, or elect voluntary registration below the threshold; (4) receive the 8-9 digit IRD number and, if registered, a 9-digit GST number; (5) enrol on myIR for electronic filing and provide New Zealand bank account details to receive any GST refunds; (6) obtain a Customs client code from the New Zealand Customs Service for physical export and import of goods. A non-resident IC with no New Zealand permanent establishment and no New Zealand-sourced assessable income is generally not required to file New Zealand income tax returns, but remains subject to GST registration obligations on taxable activities in New Zealand and to relevant indirect tax obligations on cross-border transactions.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: New Zealand does not operate a check-the-box pass-through election for companies. The IC is an entity-level taxpayer under the Income Tax Act 2007 only to the extent it derives New Zealand-sourced income through a fixed establishment or from New Zealand land, natural resources, or certain services; a tax-exempt-zone IC with no New Zealand-source taxable income is effectively outside the New Zealand income tax net. Available statutory mechanisms include: (a) voluntary GST registration under s 51(3) of the GST Act 1985 even when annual turnover is below NZD 60,000, allowing recovery of input tax on costs including acquisition of secondhand goods; (b) election of GST filing frequency (1-month, 2-month, or 6-monthly) at registration; (c) election of GST accounting basis (invoice/hybrid basis vs payments basis); (d) for non-resident suppliers of remote services, election to use the flat-rate credit scheme under s 84A of the GST Act 1985, where the non-resident supplier may claim a deemed input tax credit equal to 6/23 of the GST-inclusive consideration for specified remote/digital supplies to New Zealand consumers; and (e) hybrid mismatch limitation rules operate automatically under Subpart FH of the Income Tax Act 2007, with no elective opt-in; the IC cannot elect into or out of the hybrid rules except by structuring financing instruments to avoid hybrid outcomes.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST) under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 (value-added tax system administered by the IRD)
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 - compulsory registration for any taxable activity carried on in New Zealand when total annual taxable supplies exceed or are reasonably expected to exceed NZD 60,000 in any 12-month period; voluntary registration is permitted below the threshold. A separate NZD 60,000 threshold applies to non-resident suppliers of remote services supplied to New Zealand consumers; non-resident suppliers making such supplies are required to register and return GST unless they elect to utilise the flat-rate credit scheme where eligible.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: New Zealand imposes no real-time fiscal clearance, digital tax stamping, or API-based pre-clearance mandate. e-Invoicing is voluntary and operates on the Peppol network, administered in New Zealand under the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment's e-Invoicing programme; B2B e-invoices exchanged over Peppol are recognised for GST purposes. GST returns, GST adjustments, and GST refund claims are electronically filed through myIR. Paper or electronic tax invoices must satisfy the content requirements of ss 24-24D of the GST Act 1985, including the words 'GST invoice', supplier identity and GST number, invoice date, description and quantity of goods, consideration, and where zero-rated, the reason (e.g., 'export' or 'zero-rated under s 11'). For exported goods, the supplier must retain export evidence showing goods have left New Zealand within 28 days of the time of supply; the IRD may require presentation of this evidence in an audit.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating (0% GST) applies to supplies of goods physically exported from New Zealand by the supplier or an agent, provided the supplier holds sufficient evidence that the goods were exported within 28 days of the time of supply (s 11(1)(a), s 11(2)(a) of the GST Act 1985). For the online vintage luxury resale business, eligibility requires: (a) the goods are sold under a contract by which ownership passes to the overseas buyer; (b) the goods are delivered to an address outside New Zealand and physically removed from New Zealand within the 28-day statutory window; (c) the supplier retains the export documentation bundle; and (d) the supply, if the buyer is a New Zealand resident, is not supplied to the buyer in New Zealand. Where the IC acquires secondhand luxury goods from non-registered persons (e.g., private consignors), it may claim a secondhand goods input tax credit under s 20(3) of the GST Act 1985 equal to 3/23 of the purchase price, and the subsequent export sale is zero-rated, resulting in a net refund position. Services directly connected with exported goods (e.g., international freight, authentication and repair services supplied to non-residents) may also be zero-rated under s 11A, provided the services are supplied to a non-resident who is outside New Zealand at the time of supply and are not supplied in connection with land or moveable property in New Zealand.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: New Zealand Customs Service Electronic Export Declaration / Export Entry processed through the Trade Single Window (CusMod system)
Bill of Lading (ocean freight), Air Waybill (air freight), or courier/shipping consignment note evidencing delivery to a foreign destination
Commercial invoice and sale/purchase contract identifying the overseas buyer and showing the export consignment
Evidence of payment from the overseas buyer, including SWIFT/FX inward remittance certificate or payment gateway settlement records (Stripe/Escrow Pay settlement reports)
GST zero-rated supply evidence log recording time of supply, export date, shipping reference, and inspector/customs release number
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: The IRD may audit zero-rated export supplies and claw back input tax credits where the supplier fails to substantiate physical export within the 28-day period or where documentation is incomplete, fraudulent, or fabricated. Consequences include: (a) assessment of GST output tax at 15% on the full sale consideration, with use-of-money interest accruing from the original due date; (b) civil shortfall penalties under the Tax Administration Act 1994: 20% for failure to take reasonable care or unacceptable tax position, 40% for gross carelessness, 100% for an abusive tax position, and 150% for evasion or similar conduct; (c) late filing penalties and prosecution under s 143A of the Tax Administration Act 1994 for evasion (imprisonment up to 5 years and fines up to NZD 50,000 per offence); (d) prosecution under the Crimes Act 1961 and Customs and Excise Act 2018 for fraud, false statements, or procuring export clearance by deception; and (e) retrospective cancellation of the IC's GST registration and denial of secondhand goods input tax credits where the export chain is broken. While New Zealand has no fixed statutory FX repatriation deadline, market-standard documentary practice expects export proceeds to be repatriated within 180 days; the IRD and NZ Customs may examine the inward remittance trail as corroborative evidence that a genuine export sale occurred, and deviation from the 180-day benchmark increases audit risk.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Te Pūtea Matua)
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: New Zealand maintains a fully liberalised and freely floating currency regime, with all exchange controls abolished in 1984 under the Exchange Control Act Repeal. Both current account transactions (trade settlements, commissions, platform fees, interest, consignor payouts) and capital account transactions (equity injections, shareholder loans, dividend repatriation, liquidation proceeds) are fully convertible into NZD or any foreign currency without prior central bank approval, quantitative limits, deposit taxes, or repatriation restrictions. The New Zealand dollar (NZD) is a freely traded currency settled on the wholesale interbank market via the Continuous Linked Settlement (CLS) system. Practical compliance obligations are limited to (i) the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 (AML/CFT Act) reporting duties, which require banks to verify purpose and source of funds for cross-border wires above NZD 10,000 or of an unusual nature; and (ii) the Overseas Investment Act 2005, which is relevant only if an offshore investor acquires sensitive land or fishing quota, neither of which applies to an online consignment retail business. Profit or dividend remittance from a New Zealand-resident subsidiary would attract non-resident withholding tax at treaty-reduced or statutory rates, but in this structure the International Company is tax-exempt in its home jurisdiction and is not tax-resident in New Zealand; therefore, settlement funds held by the IC are not subject to New Zealand source taxation on conversion or repatriation.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: New Zealand imposes no statutory export proceeds surrender requirements. There is no mandated timeline for converting foreign currency export or trade receipts into NZD, no minimum conversion ratio, and no requirement to channel export earnings through any designated local account. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand does not require exporters to hedge their earnings or hold a percentage of receipts in NZD. Commercial banks may contractually require a borrower utilising trade finance facilities to repatriate sale proceeds to its NZ settlement account as a covenant of the facility, but such requirements are commercial credit conditions rather than regulatory mandates. Consequently, the CK International Company may retain USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, or CNY resale proceeds in foreign-currency accounts, convert them at market rate, or apply them to foreign supplier payables without any surrender obligation or timing constraint.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Operational Account (NZD + multi-currency sweep) and segregated Client Funds / Capital Escrow Account for consignor settlement monies
Operational Cash Management Account, Trade Finance (Documentary LC) facility, and separate Client Trust Account for escrow-backed resale proceeds
Operational Account with SWIFT-linked foreign currency sub-accounts
Business Everyday Account and Term Deposit for contingency liquidity reserve

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility rating: MEDIUM for ancillary collection and FX conversion; LOW as the primary or sole settlement rail for capital escrow obligations. Legal constraints: under the AML/CFT Act 2009, any entity providing money remittance or digital wallet services into or out of New Zealand must be registered as a reporting entity with the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA), unless it operates under a registered bank exemption. Offshore digital EMIs (e.g., Airwallex, Wise Platform, Currencycloud, Payoneer) can lawfully service a Cook Islands International Company only if the EMI (a) holds a New Zealand registered bank license (none currently do), or (b) forms an agency/trust arrangement with a locally licensed bank that performs the acceptance of deposits and NZD clearing, while the EMI provides only the interface and conversion. Most offshore EMIs will decline a zero-tax offshore International Company engaged in luxury consignment resale because (i) the beneficial ownership typically sits behind an asset-protection trust, (ii) the business model involves omnibus escrow settlements with third-party beneficial interest, and (iii) the IC lacks a New Zealand Companies Office registration. If the IC completes registration as an overseas company under section 340 of the Companies Act 1993 and appoints a New Zealand-resident agent, a niche EMI may approve onboarding but will cap monthly settlement volumes and require daily source-of-funds reporting. Overall, an EMI can be used for margin collection via card acquirers (Stripe) but not for the custody of consignor proceeds.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: New Zealand's AML/CFT Act 2009 and its associated regulations permit remote onboarding where a reporting entity applies prescribed customer due diligence (CDD) using an independent and reliable electronic identity verification source (e.g., NZ Post IdentityCheck, Jumio, or an accredited digital ID service). In practice, Reserve Bank-supervised commercial banks apply a risk-based overlay: for a tax-exempt International Company with a Cook Islands trust background and 100% non-resident ownership, the bank's financial crime committee will almost always mandate (i) an in-person meeting at the Auckland or Wellington corporate banking suite attended by at least one director or a senior authorised signatory, and (ii) a second video interview with the ultimate beneficial owner where the UBO is a trust-appointed person. The physical appearance requirement can be waived if all of the following are provided: an apostilled notarial identity pack, a live video interview on the bank's secure conferencing platform, a certified-good-standing certificate from the Cook Islands Financial Services Development Authority or the relevant registry, a formal legal opinion from New Zealand counsel on corporate authority and non-residency, and a reference letter from a regulated foreign bank where the IC maintains an existing account. Remote-only opening is therefore legally permissible but operationally rare and typically extends the onboarding period to 20–30 business days where physical appearance is waived.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Tax-exempt International Company status with no audited public filings and no Home-jurisdiction corporate tax registration
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certificate of Incorporation; Certificate of Good Standing issued within 30 days; Registered Agent attestation confirming the IC is in active status and not struck off; notarised board resolution authorising the opening of the NZ bank account and naming authorised signatories; most recent audited financial statements or, if unaudited, a CPA compilation report evidencing genuine sales revenue (e.g., invoices to luxury resale marketplaces); a New Zealand tax opinion under sections YB 4/YB 5 of the Income Tax Act 2007 confirming the company is not tax-resident in New Zealand and that no deemed source income arises on marketplace settlement funds; and a written explanation of the economic substance of the IC (physical location of inventory, number of employees, or principal function as a buying/paying vehicle).

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident beneficial ownership structured through a Cook Islands discretionary asset-protection trust, creating opacity on ultimate controller
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Complete ownership chain declaration covering every entity and natural person in the chain (bank's UBO declaration forms must be fully completed); a certified copy of the trust deed redacted only for protector's confidential drafting instructions, but disclosing the trust name, date, settlor, protector, and beneficial class; a written declaration identifying every natural person exercising direct or indirect ownership or control of at least 25% (naming the settlor or protector as the designated controller for CDD purposes); notarised and apostilled passports and proof of residential address for all identified natural persons; a Cook Islands legal opinion confirming the trust is validly constituted, is not a criminal or quasi-donation trust, and has no pending regulatory investigation; and a confirmatory letter from the trust protector consenting to disclosure of the beneficiary class to the bank on a confidential basis.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Business model is entirely online consignment of high-value secondhand luxury goods, with elevated chargeback, fraud, and anti-money laundering typology risk
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Executed marketplace or consignment agreements (e.g., with The RealReal, Vestiaire Collective, or regional auction houses) evidencing the IC's role as principal or merchant of record; a formal authentication and anti-counterfeit control narrative (third-party authenticator certification, serial-number verification tools, tamper-evident tagging, digital provenance linked to the item); statistical history of sales, returns, chargeback ratios, and average ticket value to prove a legitimate cross-border retail profile; a written AML/CFT compliance policy for the IC (even if short) covering customer screening, sanctions screening, transactional monitoring against luxury resale fraud typologies, and mitigation of stolen-goods proceeds; and an annual sales forecast and treasury estimate to contextualise expected deposit sizes and payout frequency.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Escrow_Pay and Stripe payment processing rails create commingling of consignor funds, third-party settlement risk, and ambiguity regarding the merchant of record
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: The executed Escrow Services Agreement between the IC and the escrow platform, expressly defining the IC as merchant of record and the platform as a limited-purpose payment facilitator; illustrative transactional flow diagrams showing that (i) consumer payments are captured by the platform, (ii) funds are held in a platform omnibus pool, and (iii) disbursed proceeds are receivable by the IC through a named settlement bank; a solicitor's certification that the IC is not conducting an unregistered non-bank deposit-taking business or a financial services provider under the Financial Service Providers (Registration and Dispute Resolution) Act 2008; where consignor proceeds are temporarily held in the IC's NZ bank account after settlement, a designated 'Client Funds' sub-account governed by a client money trust undertaking and audited by an external chartered accountant; and a bank-required undertaking that all chargeback and dispute liabilities remain with the IC as merchant of record, supported by a refund reserve arrangement.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Compliant routing for inbound capital: (1) Equity injection: remittance from the parent or shareholder via SWIFT MT103 to the IC's designated NZD account, with the remittance information field stating 'EQUITY CONTRIBUTION – ISSUANCE OF SHARES' and referencing the IC's entity name and internal shareholder number; the source of wealth file must include the shareholder's latest bank statement, board resolution approving the subscription, and an executed subscription agreement. (2) Shareholder loan: SWIFT MT103 labelled 'SHAREHOLDER LOAN FACILITY DRAW – [DATE] COPY OF LOAN AGREEMENT ATTACHED' ; the bank will require the signed loan agreement (governing law, interest rate, maturity, and repayment schedule) to distinguish genuine debt from equity for AML and non-resident withholding tax purposes. (3) Trade-related injections from marketplaces: SWIFT MT103 from the platform's settlement account or a regulated EMI, with remittance info 'ONLINE LUXURY RESALE SETTLEMENT – INVOICE REFERENCES [range]', accompanied by a consolidated settlement report. Verification gates: for any single inbound wire exceeding NZD 100,000 equivalent, the bank will request the underlying contract or invoice, and may file an international transaction report to the Financial Intelligence Unit; there is no overseas investment consent requirement because the capital injection does not relate to sensitive New Zealand land, fishing quota, or significant business assets. Restricted practices: never accept inbound capital from a third-party unrelated entity, over-the-counter cash, digital currency exchanges, or an account held in the name of the platform's ultimate parent without a contractual nexus, as such flows may be treated as high-risk and returned at the bank's discretion.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Clearing rails for outbound trade disbursements: (i) SWIFT MT103 (single customer credit transfer) for all supplier payments, auction house settlements, and consignor payout batches, using the IC's designated trade disbursement sub-account; beneficiaries' bank and full invoice reference are mandatory. (ii) Commercial Letters of Credit (documentary sight LC or usance LC with terms of 30–60 days) are recommended for high-value inventory acquisitions (single consignment above USD 50,000 or EUR 50,000) where the supplier requests security; the LC must be issued by the NZ clearing bank for the account of the IC and advised through the supplier's confirming bank, with presentation documents being the commercial invoice, certificate of authenticity, insurance certificate (for transit), certificate of origin, and bank-to-bank SWIFT transmission. (iii) For NZD-denominated local payments (e.g., domestic logistics, authentication vendors, local chargeback refunds), the RTGS system is the Reserve Bank's Exchange Settlement Account System (ESAS), accessed through the clearing bank with a 10:00 NZST same-day cutoff; deferred net settlement (DNS) or bulk BECS payments are acceptable only for low-value consumer refunds. (iv) For cross-border currency conversions, the bank executes an FX spot trade on the same business day as the SWIFT transfer, using a CLS-linked token to reduce settlement risk. (v) Escrow-payout batches to individual consignors should be executed through a single MT103 batch file with a consolidated payment manifest, not through card networks or instant payment apps, to preserve the audit trail. (vi) The IC must maintain sub-ledger reconciliation between marketplace settlement reports, escrow payout instructions, and bank statements, with a reconciliation cycle not exceeding T+2.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Outright FX forwards (deliverable) on NZD/USD, NZD/EUR, NZD/GBP, and NZD/JPY with maturities of one week to 12 months, documented under an ISDA 2002 Master Agreement or bank's short-form FX forward template, used strictly to hedge committed inventory purchases and payout obligations

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) for exotic or controlled currencies (e.g., offshore CNY (USD/CNH), INR, KRW) where physical delivery is impossible or the counterparty restricts settlement; NDFs are permitted to hedge underlying trade payables or receivables denominated in those currencies and must be physically evidenced by an underlying invoice

Cross-currency swaps (coupon or mark-to-market) for longer-dated balance-sheet transformation where the IC's funding currency (e.g., NZD) differs from the operating settlement currency (e.g., USD or EUR); permitted to MITIGATE structural current-asset/current-liability repricing risk arising between escrow liabilities and supplier creditors

Vanilla FX options (European or American) and zero-cost collars to protect the resale margin against adverse currency moves above preset strike levels, subject to a defined premium budget not exceeding 1.0% of hedged notional per annum and executed under the ISDA FX Annex or a bank-facilitated option confirmation

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Cook Islands Registrar of International Companies, Financial Services Supervisory Authority (FSSA) – Realm of New Zealand; filed through the licensed registered agent
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 30 calendar days following each anniversary of the date of incorporation
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: A late filing penalty accrues for each month or part-month of arrears; continued non-filing for more than 3 months permits the Registrar to publish a notice of proposed strike-off. If the default is not remedied within the notice period, the company is struck off the Register and dissolved, its assets vest in the Crown, and restoration requires a court application.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Government License and Renewal Fee
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Cook Islands Financial Services Supervisory Authority / Registrar of International Companies; collected by the licensed registered agent
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Payable on or before the anniversary of incorporation, together with the annual return; a 30-day administrative grace period applies
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Unpaid renewal fees after the grace period attract monetary penalties and loss of good standing; after three months of continuous non-payment the company may be struck off and dissolved without revenue to the Crown, and restoration is available only by court order on prescribed terms.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Beneficial Ownership Confirmation and Register Update
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Licensed registered agent maintaining the confidential beneficial ownership register; available to the Registrar on statutory request
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Submitted annually with the annual return and promptly upon any change in shareholding or control, in all cases within 15 days after the change
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to provide or update beneficial ownership information is an offence under the international companies regime; a monetary penalty may be imposed, the registered agent may resign, and the company may lose valid standing and become liable to strike-off.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No statutory audit is required for an International Company that is tax-exempt, does not carry on business in the Cook Islands, holds no Cook Islands land, and has not entered into a regulated domestic activity. The Registrar may require an independent audit where the company transacts business with Cook Islands residents or where an irregularity is suspected.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: No statutory filing of financial statements is required; accounts may be prepared under IFRS, US GAAP, or another recognised GAAP at the directors' discretion. Complete books and records must be maintained to explain transactions and financial position and must be kept for at least 7 years.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Annually, the licensed registered agent must obtain a beneficial ownership declaration identifying each registrable beneficial owner and any changes in shareholding or control. A confidential beneficial ownership register is maintained at the registered office and is not open to public inspection, but must be disclosed to the Registrar upon lawful request.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Minute Book of shareholder and director meetings
Register of Beneficial Owners (confidential, maintained by registered agent)

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No general statutory tax holiday exists in New Zealand. A non-resident International Company (IC) that is not incorporated in NZ, has no permanent establishment (PE), and derives no NZ-source income is subject to nil NZ corporate income tax (tax-exempt zone outcome). Where NZ-source income is derived, the effective rate is reduced by imputation credits (fully imputed dividends 15% NRWT) and by DTA-reduced rates (e.g., royalties 10%, interest 10% or 2% under the Approved Issuer Levy). An R&D Tax Incentive of 15% refundable tax credit applies to eligible NZ R&D expenditure. Loss carry-forward is indefinite under s IA 4 Income Tax Act 2007, subject to the 49% continuity of ownership and same-or-similar business test.
corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_loss_carryforward_rule: Indefinite — s IA 4 Income Tax Act 2007 imposes no 5-year cap; losses are carried forward subject to a 49% continuity of ownership threshold and a same-or-similar business test. The 5-year figure in the schema is a generic pipeline bracket, not a New Zealand statutory limit.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: IR4 – Company Income Tax Return, filed electronically via the Inland Revenue 'MyIR' secure web portal. Tax agents may file via ARTS (Agent Revenue Tax System) or IRD-approved commercial software (e.g., Xero, MYOB). The official line-by-line guide is IR4G (IR4 Guide).
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual. Taxable year is the New Zealand income year; standard balance date is 31 March. Provisional tax liabilities are paid through three 6-monthly instalments during the year. GST, if registered, is filed separately on a 1-, 2-, or 6-monthly cycle.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: IR4 is due on the 7th day of the second month after balance date (31 March balance date → due 7 July). For a company with a registered tax agent, Inland Revenue extends the filing date to the 31st day of the third month after the terminal tax date (usually 31 March following the income year), and terminal tax is payable by 7 April under the extension regime.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Gross NZ-source revenue from the online consignment of vintage luxury goods, including proceeds from Stripe, Escrow_Pay, and other payment rails before commissions and chargebacks.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report only gross income sourced in New Zealand (s YD 4 source rules). Revenue generated by a non-resident IC with no NZ PE and no NZ-resident agent is not subject to NZ income tax and is omitted. If the IC is deemed to have an NZ PE through an agent taking orders in NZ, all attributable NZ gross turnover must be disclosed.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: IR4 Line 2 – Interest, dividends, and other income
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: NZ-sourced interest, dividends, royalties, and other miscellaneous income received by the company during the income year.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Disclose NZ-sourced dividends, interest, and royalties before NRWT/RWT. A non-resident IC may be able to treat the amounts as grossed-up for foreign tax credit purposes or claim treaty-exempt treatment; attached RWT/NRWT credits are claimed at Line 9.
Total reportable NZ-source income; the same figure carries to the tax reconciliation schedule.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Expenses incurred in deriving the taxable NZ-source income, including cost of goods sold, freight, customs/GST on imported inventory, fulfilment, marketing, platform fees, and chargebacks.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-residents may claim only expenses necessarily incurred in producing NZ-source income and apportioned on a reasonable basis. Head-office overheads and offshore marketing costs are deductible only if evidenced and attributed to the NZ income-earning activity; otherwise they are disallowed.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Line 3 minus Line 4; the accounting-tax adjusted net result before tax adjustments.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: If a loss arises, NZ loss carry-forward rules apply; non-resident ICs with no NZ PE cannot generally establish a loss ring-fenced to NZ-sourced activity.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax adjustments such as loss carry-forward/offset, capital allowances, non-deductible entertainment, or subpart FV/CFC inclusions.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident IC must include any attributable CFC inclusion or income-tracking adjustments; generally nil in a clean tax-exempt zone structure.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Line 5 adjusted by Line 6; the amount subject to NZ corporate income tax at 28%.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Where no NZ PE exists and only NZ-source withholding income was reported, taxable income is generally nil or an amount equal to the net of grossed-up NZ-source passive income; treaty protections must be evidenced in the return notes.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: IR4 Line 8 – Tax on taxable income
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Income tax at the 28% corporate rate applied to taxable income (Line 7).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident ICs with no NZ PE and no NZ-source income will have a nil amount here.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Credits for resident withholding tax, non-resident withholding tax, and imputation credits attached to NZ dividends.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Claim credits only where the IC is assessable on the underlying gross NZ-source income; a non-resident that is exempt due to a DTA or absence of a PE cannot claim imputation credits and instead receives the income gross or with reduced NRWT.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Line 8 less Line 9; net tax due or refundable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Refunds for non-residents are remitted via MyIR to the nominated NZ bank account or by international wire; a non-resident must hold a valid IRD number and provide an overseas address to claim a refund.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty: NZ$250 for a company (TAA s 139A), with an additional subsequent late filing penalty for returns outstanding more than 12 months after the due date. Late payment penalty: an initial penalty of 1% of the unpaid amount on the day after the due date, then an incremental 4% per month (TAA s 139B) on the unpaid remainder; Use-of-Money Interest (UOMI) accrues daily at the IRD-prescribed underpayment rate. Shortfall penalties for incorrect returns: 20% (lack of reasonable care), 40% (gross carelessness), 100% (abusive tax position), and 150% (evasion). A failure to furnish a return is an offence under s 143A TAA, with fines up to NZ$25,000 for a first offence.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: Non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) on dividends: 30% on non-fully-imputed dividends; 15% on fully imputed dividends. Under DTA (e.g., NZ-Australia, NZ-UK), the treaty rate is reduced to 5% where the beneficial owner is a company holding at least 10% of the voting power and the dividend qualifies for full imputation/credit attachment; otherwise the treaty rate is generally 15%.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke DTA relief, the non-resident recipient must obtain a Certificate of Residence (IRD Form IR290) endorsed by the competent authority of the treaty jurisdiction and deliver it to the NZ withholding payer before the dividend/royalty/interest payment is made. Where the treaty requires a minimum shareholding, a shareholder declaration (beneficial owner name, address, shareholding percentage, and treaty residence) must accompany the IR290. The payer must retain these documents for seven years. If NRWT is over-withheld despite a valid IR290, the non-resident may file a refund claim (IR3NR or IR4) or use IRD Form IR292 for an early refund of excess NRWT; the claim must be made within the statutory time limits under s 342 TAA.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Royalties: statutory NRWT 15%; DTA rates commonly 10% (e.g., US 10%, UK 10%, China 10%) and 5% under certain treaties for industrial/commercial/scientific equipment royalties (e.g., Australia 5% for such equipment). Interest: statutory NRWT 15%; the Approved Issuer Levy (AIL) reduces the effective cost to 2% where the NZ borrower is an approved issuer, no associated-party non-resident loan relationship exists, and the interest is not otherwise subject to NZ income tax; DTA rates for interest generally range from 10% to 15% depending on the treaty.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Contemporaneous New Zealand transfer pricing documentation (Master File and Local File) is required where the multinational group has annual global turnover of NZ$100 million or more and the NZ-resident entity (or NZ PE of a non-resident) enters into cross-border related-party transactions (including inventory purchases and management fees) exceeding NZ$10 million in an income year. The Inland Revenue International Questionnaire (IR1061) is the standard disclosure mechanism for such transactions. Transactions below these thresholds remain subject to the arm's length standard under s GC 13 and require contemporaneous evidence upon request.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand does not maintain Caribbean-style Economic Substance Regulations. Substance nevertheless controls the tax outcome through: (i) tax residence of a company under s YD 2 (incorporation in NZ or centre of management in NZ); (ii) the permanent establishment threshold under ss YD 4 and YD 5; (iii) the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR) in s BG 1; (iv) the Taxation (Neutralising Base Erosion and Profit Shifting) Act 2018, which denies benefits to related-party financing and platform structures lacking sufficient people, functions, assets, and risks; and (v) the Multilateral Instrument (MLI) Principal Purpose Test for treaty access. An IC that merely holds title to vintage luxury inventory while all sales, marketing, customer support, and risk functions are performed in New Zealand will be found to have a dependent agent PE of the foreign principal, attributing taxable profit to New Zealand.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion / Fraudulent Returns – Tax Administration Act 1994 ss 143A-143B
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Knowingly or recklessly filing an IR4 return that omits NZ-source income from online sales of vintage luxury goods; fabricating consignment records to inflate deductions; concealing Stripe/Escrow_Pay settlement data; using undisclosed offshore bank accounts; or instructing a tax agent to file false tax returns.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Criminal conviction: for an individual, imprisonment up to 5 years and/or a fine up to NZ$50,000; for a company, a fine up to NZ$50,000. Civil shortfall penalty of 150% of the evaded tax plus Use-of-Money Interest; the time bar for reassessment is extended indefinitely where evasion exists; the Crown may also seek forfeiture of proceeds of crime under the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act 2009.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and shadow directors are prosecuted as principals for the company's false return. Personal civil restitution may be ordered for the tax shortfall; director disqualification up to 5 years under s 382 Companies Act 1993; travel bans are available where fugitive or flight risk is shown in an insolvency examination or arrest warrant procedure under the Insolvency Act 2006; imprisonment up to 5 years is personal.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Sham / Shell Company & General Anti-Avoidance – s BG 1 Income Tax Act 2007
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating the IC as a non-resident brass-plate re-invoicing vehicle with no New Zealand office, employees, bank account, local management, or business substance, while the online luxury resale platform, customer relationships, inventory risk, and vendor contracts are managed in New Zealand; artificially booking the resale margin offshore to avoid the 28% corporate rate; disregarding NZ PE rules.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The Commissioner may reconstruct the arrangement under the GAAR: ignore the IC as a sham intermediary, attribute the full resale margin to the New Zealand principal/settlor, and assess tax at 28% plus an abusive tax position shortfall penalty of 100% and UOMI. The IC's local registered office/agent may be prosecuted for facilitating a sham; deregistration and striking off under the Companies Act 1993 may follow.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: The corporate veil is pierced for fraud or sham: directors are jointly and severally liable for the avoided tax as parties to the sham. Personal civil restitution orders, disqualification from managing companies, and, in liquidation, examination orders under s 261 Companies Act 1993 may compel the director's attendance, production of records, and surrender of passport; non-compliance leads to arrest. Criminal conspiracy charges may result in imprisonment up to 5 years.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: AML/CFT Non-Compliance – Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating as a dealer in high-value goods (defined as accepting NZ$15,000 or more in cash for luxury goods) or as an online marketplace without an AML/CFT programme; failing to conduct customer due diligence and enhanced ongoing due diligence for medium-risk clients; failing to report suspicious transactions involving vintage handbags, watches, or jewellery; structuring cash payments into sub-threshold amounts to avoid reporting (smurfing); allowing Escrow_Pay transactions to facilitate vendor money laundering.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Civil penalty up to NZ$2 million for a body corporate per contravention; criminal penalty for an individual: fine up to NZ$5 million and/or imprisonment up to 2 years; corporate fine up to NZ$5 million; enforcement includes remediation orders, suspension or conditions on business registration, and forfeiture of proceeds of crime under the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act 2009.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors, senior managers, and compliance officers are 'designated persons' under the AML/CFT Act. They may be personally liable for civil penalties where they aided, abetted, or failed to supervise an employee's contravention (s 100); criminal liability attaches where they knowingly permit money laundering. The court may prohibit a person from holding a directorship in any reporting entity; travel bans may be imposed in criminal proceedings when the director poses a flight risk; imprisonment up to 2 years is a personal sanction.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing and Thin Capitalisation Non-Observance – Income Tax Act 2007 ss GC 13, GC 15
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Purchasing vintage luxury inventory from an offshore associate at inflated prices and reselling at thin margins; routing platform fees or IP royalties to a low-tax jurisdiction without the substance to support the charge; failing to prepare contemporaneous Master File and Local File where cross-border related-party transactions exceed NZ$10 million and group turnover exceeds NZ$100 million; back-to-back intercompany loans with excessive interest deductions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Transfer pricing adjustment to the arm's length price under s GC 13; shortfall penalty of 20% for an unacceptable tax position escalating to 40% for gross carelessness, 100% for an abusive position, and 150% for evasion; UOMI on the underpayment; mandatory disclosure via IR1061; possible NRWT recapture on adjusted cross-border payments.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who approved the non-arm's length pricing and signed the return may be assessed personally for failure to exercise due diligence; civil restitution of the shortfall is recoverable as a Crown debt. In insolvency, the liquidator may sue directors for reckless or negligent trading (ss 135 and 137 Companies Act 1993) for causing the company to incur an uneconomic tax liability; deliberate manipulation constitutes evasion, leading to imprisonment up to 5 years.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Profit Repatriation and Withholding Tax Defaults – Income Tax Act 2007 ss NG 1, RF 8
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Declaring a dividend to the non-resident parent or to the IC without withholding NRWT; incorrectly applying the 15% fully imputed rate where no imputation credits are attached; paying royalties to a related offshore IP-holding shell without a documented licence or at non-arm's length values; using the Approved Issuer Levy for an interest payment that does not qualify (e.g., to an associated non-resident lender); failing to file an NRWT return in the month following the distribution.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The company, as agent, is personally liable for the un-withheld NRWT under s RF 8, together with the initial 1% late payment penalty, monthly 4% increments, and UOMI; shortfall penalties up to 150% apply for deliberate failure to withhold; unpaid NRWT constitutes a Crown debt ranking ahead of unsecured creditors in liquidation; late filing penalties for NRWT returns apply per return.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Under s 151 TAA, directors and former directors of a company that fails to pay withholding tax (including NRWT) after receiving a 30-day demand may be personally liable for the entire unpaid amount, without limitation, where they have failed to procure payment or place the company in liquidation; personal civil restitution, director disqualification, and, in cases of fraudulent diversion of withheld tax, imprisonment up to 5 years and travel bans in extradition proceedings.
